newsitem.title: USA: Whitewater prosecutor demands White House notes.
newsitem.headline: Whitewater prosecutor demands White House notes.

text.p: The Whitewater prosecutor told the U.S. Supreme Court on Thursday the White House should be forced to turn over notes of converations between government lawyers and first lady Hillary Rodham Clinton.

Whitewater independent counsel Kenneth Starr said in a 30-page filing with the high court that the White House cannot assert attorney-client privilege to shield the notes, which he demanded in a grand jury subpoena a year ago.

"The White House has produced reams of attorney notes virtually identical to those at issue here, including attorney notes addressing the same subject matters. The only difference here is that these notes reflect communications with Mrs. Clinton," he said.
Starr specifically cited the turning over of notes of communications by government attorneys with Bernard Nussbaum and Margaret Williams when they were top White House aides.
Starr said the notes were relevant to the grand jury's investigation of "several present or former White House officers and employees." He did not identify those under investigation.

Starr has been conducting a lengthy investigation into the Whitewater affair, a complex web of Arkansas business deals involving the Clintons, and allegations of a later coverup. President Bill Clinton and his wife have not been accused of any wrongdoing.

One set of notes was based on what Mrs. Clinton told White House lawyers about her grand jury testimony on Jan. 26, 1996, when she said she did not know how Whitewater-related legal billing records ended up in the White House residence.

Another set of notes, dated July 11, 1995, concerned her activities right after the July 1993 suicide of White House lawyer Vince Foster, who worked with Mrs. Clinton at a law firm in Little Rock when her husband was governor of Arkansas.

Starr's filing occurred just two days after the Supreme Court handed the president a stunning defeat, ruling unanimously that Paula Jones' sexual harassment lawsuit can proceed now rather than wait until he leaves office.

In asking the justices to deny the appeal, Starr said, "What the case presents, at bottom, is a bold assertion of a governmental privilege against a federal grand jury's interest in securing relevant evidence."

He said that granting the White House's appeal "would delay a highly sensitive criminal investigation; indeed, several parts of the investigation could remain frozen for an additional three to 12 months."
Starr said a U.S. appeals court ruling requiring that the White House surrender the notes was "thoroughly and soundly grounded in law and public policy."
He said U.S. law requires that any federal government agency, including the White House, must provide to law enforcement authorities "any information" relating to criminal violations.
Starr argued that government attorneys and employees know their communications and work may be disclosed if relevant to a federal criminal investigation.

Besides, he said the claim of attorney-client privilege fails because Mrs. Clinton is not a government officer or employee, and the notes involved Whitewater matters, not governmental duties assigned to the first lady.
If the Supreme Court decides to grant the appeal, Starr requested that oral arguments be scheduled as soon as possible. But the court was not expected to hear the case until October at the earliest.
The justices are due to decide by the end of next month whether to hear or to reject the White House appeal.
